'''{{ill|Iwatoyama Kofun|ja|岩戸山古墳|zh|岩戶山古墳|qid=Q11474582}}''' is a {{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|qid=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun}} located in {{ill|Yame|ar|يامي (فوكوكا)|azb|یامه، فوکوئوکا|ce|Яме (гӀала)|ceb|Yame Shi|de|Yame|es|Yame (Fukuoka)|fa|یامه، فوکوئوکا|fi|Yame|fr|Yame|gl|Yame|hak|Yame, Fukuoka|id|Yame, Fukuoka|it|Yame|ja|八女市|ko|야메시|my|ယမဲမြို့၊ ဖုခုအိုခ|mzn|یامه، فوکوئوکا|nl|Yame|pl|Yame|pt|Yame|ro|Yame|ru|Яме (город)|sv|Yame|tg|Яме|tl|Yame (Fukuoka)|tr|Yame|tt|Яме (шәһәр)|uk|Яме|ur|یامے ، فوکوکا|vi|Yame, Fukuoka|war|Yame, Fukuoka|zh|八女市|zh_classical|八女市|zh_min_nan|Yame-chhī|zh_yue|八女|qid=Q850492|lt=Yame, Fukuoka}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|qid=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture}}, Japan. It is part of the {{ill|Yame Kofun Cluster|ja|八女古墳群|qid=Q64615207|lt=Yame Kofun Cluster}} and has been designated as a {{ill|Historic site|en|Historic site|qid=Q1081138|lt=Historic site of Japan}}} (under the collective designation "Yame Kofun Cluster"). It is the largest kofun in northern {{ill|Kyushu|ja|九州地方}}<ref group="note">The largest kofun in Kyushu is {{ill|Mezasahozuka Kofun|ja|女狭穂塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nyōsazuka Kofun|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 女狭穂塚古墳|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11446520}} in Miyazaki Prefecture, with a total length of 176m.</ref> and is estimated to have been constructed in the early {{ill|6th century|af|6de eeu|als|6. == Overview ==
[[File:Iwatoyama-kofun zenkei.JPG|thumb|250px|right|{{center|Full view of Iwatoyama Kofun}}{{small|Foreground: keyhole front section, Background: round rear section.}}]]
[[File:Iwatoyama-kofun Daijinguu.JPG|thumb|250px|right|{{center|Daijinguu shrine adjacent to the tumulus.}}]]
{{ill|Iwatoyama Kofun|ja|岩戸山古墳|zh|岩戶山古墳|qid=Q11474582}} is situated in the northern area of Yame City on the Yame Hills. These hills span approximately 10 kilometers east to west and are home to numerous kofun dating from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref group="note">While most kofun here date from the 5th to 6th centuries, the range includes square moated tombs from the early 4th century to circular kofun from the early 7th century ("Iwatoyama Historical Museum Exhibit Catalog," p. 9).</ref> Among the approximately 300 Kofuns, including 12 keyhole-shaped kofun and three decorated kofun, Iwatoyama Kofun is one of the most prominent.<ref>"Iwatoyama Historical Museum Exhibit Catalog," p. 9.</ref>

The kofun is oriented along an east-west axis, with its circular rear mound facing east. It features a two-tiered construction and includes a unique square section known as "Bekkū" (別区), measuring 43 meters on each side, located at the northeast corner.<ref name="exhibit16">"Iwatoyama Historical Museum Exhibit Catalog," p. 16.</ref> Based on the dating of {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|qid=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, it is estimated to have been built in the early 6th century, aligning with historical records of {{ill|Tsukushi no Kimi Iwai|ja|筑紫君磐井}} (also known as {{ill|Chikushi Kimi Iwai|ja|筑紫君磐井}}).<ref name="exhibit16"/> Although the internal structure is unknown, geophysical surveys suggest the presence of a {{ill|horizontal stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室}}.<ref name="exhibit16"/> A shrine (Daijingū) stands near the tumulus, which originally occupied the top of the circular mound.

The tumulus, surrounding moat, and Bekkū have yielded over 100 stone burial goods, collectively referred to as "stone humans and horses" ({{ill|Sekijin sekiba|en|Sekijin sekiba|qid=Q17994947|lt=Sekijin sekiba}}). These burial goods, which are unique to the area, fall into three categories: human figures, animals, and utensils. Most are life-sized.<ref name="exhibit16"/> Replicas of these stone burial goods, scaled down, are now displayed in Bekkū.

Iwatoyama Kofun was designated as a National Historic Site on December 23, 1955. The Historic site was expanded and unified into the "Yame Kofun Group" on March 24, 1978.<ref>"Illustrated Guide to Japan's Historic sites, Volume 3" (Dōhōsha Publishing, 1991), p. 206.</ref><ref group="note">The historic sites "Iwatoyama Kofun," "{{ill|Noriba Kofun|ja|乗場古墳|lt=Nobaba Kofun}}," "{{ill|Sekijinzan Kofun|ja|石人山古墳}}," "{{ill|Zenzōzuka Kofun|ja|善蔵塚古墳}}," and "{{ill|Kōkadani Kofun|ja|弘化谷古墳}}" were unified, with three additional kofun ({{ill|Maruyamazuka Kofun|ja|丸山塚古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Maruyamazuka Kofun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17503167}}, {{ill|Maruyama Kofun (Yame)|ja|丸山古墳 (八女市)}}, and {{ill|Chausuzuka Kofun|ja|茶臼塚古墳}}) added.</ref>

== Kofun area ==
* Total length: Over 170 meters
* Mound length: Approximately 135 meters
* Circular rear mound:
** Diameter: Approximately 60 meters
** Height: Approximately 18 meters
* Rectangular front mound:
** Width: Approximately 92 meters
** Height: Approximately 17 meters
* Bekkū:
** Square area with 43-meter sides

A moat and embankment 20 meters wide surround the tumulus.<ref name="exhibit16"/>

== Burial ==
The interred is believed to be {{ill|Tsukushi no Kimi Iwai|ja|筑紫君磐井}} (also known as {{ill|Chikushi Kimi Iwai|ja|筑紫君磐井}}), a regional ruler of northern Kyushu in the early 6th century. This kofun is one of the few in Japan where burial and construction dates can be estimated based on historical documents.<ref name="exhibit16"/>

{{ill|Tsukushi no Kimi Iwai|ja|筑紫君磐井}} is noted in the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|qid=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}} for leading a rebellion (see {{ill|Iwai Rebellion|en|Iwai Rebellion|qid=Q3138004|lt=Iwai Rebellion}}). The {{ill|Chikugo-no-Kuni Fudoki|qid=Q135505754}} fragment describes the kofun and its location, including references to judicial-like functions in Bekkū.<ref name="exhibit16"/> According to this account, Iwai began constructing his tomb during his lifetime but abandoned it after losing a battle.

Previously, {{ill|Sekijinzan Kofun|ja|石人山古墳}} was thought to be Iwai's tomb. This was revised by scholar Sadashirō Mori in 1956, and Iwatoyama Kofun is now widely accepted as his final resting place.

== Related Cultural Assets ==
* Stone human figure ({{ill|Tokyo National Museum|en|Tokyo National Museum|qid=Q653433|lt=Tokyo National Museum}}, {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|qid=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property}})<ref>Ministry of Education, Science, and Culture Notification No. 106, June 5, 1976.</ref>
* Two stone human figures, one stone quiver, and two stone shields with attached fragments (Yame City, stored at Iwatoyama Historical Cultural Exchange Hall, Important Cultural Property)<ref>Ministry of Education, Science, and Culture Notification No. 108, June 29, 2010.</ref>
* Stone horse, armored human head, and two stone human fragments (traditionally from Iwatoyama Kofun, owned by Shōfuku-ji, Yame City, and Fukuoka Prefecture Designated Tangible Cultural Property)<ref>[http://www.city.yame.fukuoka.jp/kanko/8/1496969698028.html "Cultural Assets of Yame City"] (Yame City website, accessed December 17, 2020).</ref>
